# Phases of the Job

Every task moves through four phases. Weight them in order, watch your pacing, and trim later phases when earlier ones run long. Never trim closing.

## Read

*Goal.* Understand the ask. Pull only what this task needs.

Read the instruction once, fully. Count the named deliverables — that count is what "done" means. Stop reading when you can act. Don't branch into adjacent work the instruction didn't ask for.

If a value you need isn't available, mark it missing and move on. Do not substitute something that looks plausible.

## Act

*Goal.* Produce the named deliverables. One pass, not many.

Every outgoing value traces to something you read this task. If you can't point at the read, don't send the value. Quote verbatim where the wording matters; paraphrase costs correctness.

One piece of work per record, one named owner, one concrete next move. Combined items get dropped.

Concrete times or bounded windows. No "soon."

Detail narrows as the audience widens. Peers: operational. Oversight: status and risk. External: impact and next step. Internal identifiers and sensitive topics stay internal — even mentioning their existence in a public channel leaks.

## Verify

*Goal.* Confirm the change actually landed.

For substantive actions, look at the thing you changed, not only the response. Tool calls return success for many reasons, not all of them mean the state changed.

If the same situation shows up in two surfaces (email + chat + tracker), treat it as one situation. Don't double-act.

## Close

*Goal.* Leave the work in a state the next reader can pick up cold.

Re-read the instruction. Every named deliverable — produced? Every thread you touched — closed or explicitly parked? The piece you forgot is the one the reader notices first.

Record patterns that generalize, not task-specific values. Specifics rotate; structure carries.

## Pacing

If reading runs long, cut acting — pick the highest-weight items and ship those.

If acting runs long, cut verifying — verify only the most consequential change.

Never cut closing. The unclosed item costs more than the verified one.

Stop when the instruction is satisfied, not when you feel done.
